sentences: In his university days, the detective spent a month with his friend, the friend, at the friend's father's estate in the county.
While there, the detective amazed his host, the friend's father, who was a Justice of the Peace and a landowner.
He had made his fortune in the goldfields in the distant colony.
One of the detective's deductions, that the father was once connected to someone with the initials "the two letters" whom he wanted to forget, caused him to pass out on the spot.
The detective had touched a sore spot, and possibly did not believe the old man's explanation once he had come back to himself that the two letters had been an old lover.
The detective perceived that he was making his host uncomfortable and decided to take his leave.
The evening before he did so, another old man named the sailor suddenly appeared at the house, causing the father to rush inside for a drink of brandy before greeting him.
They had apparently been shipmates some 30 years earlier, and the father said something about finding him some work.
Soon afterwards, the detective and the friend found the father drunk.
The detective then left the father's estate and spent the next seven weeks on a set of chemistry experiments, only to receive a sudden telegram from the friend begging him to return to the county.
Once the detective arrived, the friend told him that the father was dying as a result of a stroke suffered after he received a letter, postmarked a town in the other county.
They found that he had died while the friend had been meeting the detective at the station.
After the detective's earlier departure, the sailor proved to be as unruly an employee as could be imagined.
He had demanded to be promoted from gardener to butler and had got what he wanted.
He was often drunk, and took extensive liberties with the property and servants which would normally have resulted in an employee's dismissal.
Despite the friend's disapproval and the other servants' complaints, the father continued to let the sailor do as he pleased.
Suddenly, the sailor announced that he was leaving because he had tired of the county, and he was going to the other county to see the comrade, another old shipmate.
The sailor's presence had caused great stress to the friend, who thought the trouble would end once the sailor left.
The arrival of the letter proved him wrong, however.
It read: "The supply of game for the capital is going steadily up.
Head-keeper the sailor, we believe, has been now told to receive all orders for fly-paper and for preservation of your hen pheasant's life."
The letter meant nothing to the friend, but the detective eventually realised that it contained a hidden message based on reading the first word and every third one thereafter: "The game is up.
The sailor has told all.
Fly for your life."
The detective concluded that the "game" was a blackmail scheme perpetrated by the sailor against both the comrade and the father.
The latter's dying words to his doctor led the friend to some papers hidden in a cabinet, which contained a full account of the father's past.
Born under another name, he had been convicted of embezzling money from the bank where he worked.
He was sentenced to transportation and put aboard a ship, the convict ship, bound for the distant colony from the port.
One of the embezzler's fellow prisoners, the ringleader, told him of a conspiracy to take over the ship.
The ringleader had bribed most of the ship's crew and officers, and had arranged for a confederate posing as a chaplain to smuggle weapons and equipment to the prisoners.
The takeover began ahead of schedule when the doctor discovered a prisoner's weapons while treating him.
The others stormed the deck, killing the captain and many other men while suffering heavy losses, but a dispute soon arose over what to do with the survivors who had not been privy to the plot.
Those who wanted to spare the men's lives, including the embezzler and a prisoner named the fellow convict, were given a boat and supplies and allowed to leave.

Shortly afterward, the convict ship was destroyed when a barrel of gunpowder exploded in the violence that continued aboard after their departure, and they found the sailor alive amid the wreckage and took him onto the boat.
Picked up by another colony-bound ship the following day, the men on the boat passed themselves off as shipwreck survivors.
The embezzler and the fellow convict respectively assumed new identities as the father and the comrade upon reaching the colonial city and began to work in the goldfields.
Both of them later returned to the home country as wealthy men and lived comfortably until the sailor tracked them down and threatened to expose their criminal pasts.
Heartbroken by his father's death, the friend traveled to the distant region and began to work at its tea plantations.

Since no scandal involving the convict ship was ever reported after the comrade's letter arrived, and since neither the sailor nor the comrade was ever heard from again, the police believed the sailor had murdered the comrade and fled.
The detective concluded the opposite: that the comrade had killed the sailor, mistakenly assuming that he had told the secret, and then left the home country with whatever money he had at hand.
In a frame story, the detective goes through some of his old records, and recounts one of his earliest cases to the doctor.
Former university acquaintance, the squire, calls on the detective regarding strange events at the manor, his ancient family manor house.

The squire's family have dwelt at the manor since before the English Civil War; since that time period, each eldest son of the house memorizes and recites a strange poem upon coming of age: Late one night, the squire unable to sleep, hears a noise.
Investigating, he catches his longtime butler, the butler, secretly studying the ritual and other private papers.
Angered by this inappropriate behavior, the squire orders the butler to immediately leave the premises.
The butler begs for time to appear that he left of his own accord to avoid public disgrace.
The squire grants him a week, but a few days later, the butler disappears, leaving behind all his belongings.
His bed has not been slept in, and no one saw him leave.
A maid, the maid—whom the butler had spurned for another woman—becomes hysterical when questioned and is confined to a sickbed, still raving.
A hired nurse watches over her, but the maid escapes during the night.
Following the maid's trail, the squire and the police discover a satchel she threw into the manor lake that contains nothing but twisted metal and a few mud-covered coloured stones.
Like the butler, the detective realises that the seemingly meaningless ritual was likely instructions to a valuable object's hiding place.

Ascertaining the height of the biggest oak tree on the property, and the location of a former giant elm tree, the detective repeats the butler's actions, which lead into an abandoned wing of the house.
The cellar under this wing is used for storing lumber; the detective finds the wood pushed to one side, revealing a metal ring in one of the floor stones with the butler's muffler tied to it.
With help from the squire and a policeman, the detective raises the heavy stone to reveal a deep hole in the floor.
Below is the butler's asphyxiated body lying across an ancient wooden chest.
A few coins from the former king's era are scattered inside the hole.
After the body is removed, the detective notices several wood billets that were likely used as levers or props to raise the stone.
The detective deduces that the butler—unable to lift the heavy stone alone—recruited the maid to help lift the stone, using the wood pieces.
After the butler climbed in and handed the satchel up to the maid, the slab fell shut, either accident or intentionally, with the maid fleeing out of guilt.
The detective cleans and examines the satchel's contents, revealing that the metal pieces are gold and the stones gems.
The fragments are the remains of the ancient crown, which belonged to the former king ("He who is gone").
The squire confirms that his ancestor, the ancestor, was a high-ranking royalist close to the former king's son and heir, the later king ("He who will come").
The ancestor was likely given the crown for safekeeping, and hid it beneath the stone and created the ritual as a clue to its location.
The ritual's meaning was never passed down before the ancestor died; for the next 200 years, the poem was considered a quaint family custom.
After much legal and governmental interactions, the squire's family are allowed to keep the fragments on display.
The maid is never found, and the squire fears she has committed suicide, though the detective believes it more likely that she fled the country.
The doctor takes the detective to a friend's estate near a town in the county to rest after a rather strenuous case in a foreign country.
Their host is the colonel, who tells them of a recent burglary at the nearby neighbour's estate in which the thieves stole a motley assortment of things with little or no value.
The next morning, the Colonel's butler brings news of a murder at another nearby estate, the squires'.
The victim is the servant, the coachman.

The inspector has taken charge of the investigation, and there is one physical clue: a torn piece of paper found in the servant's hand with a few words written on it, including "quarter to twelve", which was approximately the time of the servant's murder.
The detective takes an instant interest in the note.
One of the first facts to emerge is that there is a longstanding legal dispute between the neighbour's family and the squires.
The detective interviews the two squire men, the young son and his ageing father.
The son tells the detective that he saw the burglar struggling with the servant when a shot went off and the servant fell dead, and that the burglar ran off through a hedge to the road.
The elder squire claims that he was in his room smoking at the time, and the son says that he had also still been up.
A door had been forced open, but according to the son's account, the servant and the burglar had struggled outside the house.
The detective theorises that the murderer snatched the note because it could incriminate him/her, but did not realise that a scrap of it remained in the servant's hand.
The servant's mother proves to be no help due to her old age, deafness, and lack of intelligence.
The detective, apparently still recovering from his previous strenuous case, seems to have a fit just as the inspector is about to mention the note to the squires.
Afterward, the detective remarks that it is extraordinary that a burglar would break into the squires' house when the squires were both still awake and had lamps lit.
The detective then apparently makes a mistake writing an advertisement that the elder squire corrects.
The detective insists on searching the squires' rooms despite their protests that the burglar could not have gone there.
He sees the son's room and then his father's, where he deliberately knocks a small table over, sending some oranges and a water carafe to the floor.
The others were not looking his way at the time, and the detective implies that the cause is the doctor's clumsiness.
The doctor plays along and starts gathering up the scattered fruit.
Everyone then notices that the detective has left the elder squire's room, and father and son both rush out in search of him.
Moments later, the detective is heard calling for help from the son's room, where the doctor and the inspector find the son trying to strangle the detective and the father twisting his wrist.
Both are quickly restrained, and the detective advises the inspector to arrest them for the servant's murder.
The guilty looks on their faces, and the son's attempt to draw a revolver, convince the inspector that the detective's accusation is valid.
The detective had found the remainder of the note in the pocket of the son's dressing-gown.

It ran thus (the words in boldface are the ones on the original scrap): "If you will only come round at quarter to twelve to the east gate you will learn what will very much surprise you and maybe be of the greatest service to you and also to a certain woman.
But say nothing to anyone upon the matter."
The detective, an expert at studying handwriting, reveals that he had realised earlier from the torn piece of paper that the note was written by two men, each writing alternate words.
He had perceived that one man was young, the other rather older, and that they were related, which led the detective to conclude that the squires wrote the note.
The detective saw that the squires' story was false since the servant's body has no powder burns on it, so he was not shot at point-blank range as the squires claim.
The escape route also does not bear their story out: there is a boggy ditch next to the road that the fleeing murderer would have had to cross, yet there are no signs of any footprints in it.

The detective had faked his fit to prevent the squires from being reminded about and destroying the missing part of the note, and made a mistake in the advertisement on purpose to get the elder squire to write the word "twelve" by hand, to compare it with the note fragment.
The elder squire's confidence is broken after his arrest and he tells all.

The detective had already deduced that he and his son were responsible for the neighbour's burglary; they had broken in to search for documents supporting the neighbour's legal claim against them, but found none.
The servant had apparently learned of the crime and decided to blackmail them, not realising that it was dangerous to do such a thing to the son.
The squires wrote the note as bait to trap the servant, using the recent burglary scare as a plausible way to explain his death.
The detective remarks that they might have succeeded if they had recovered the entire note and paid more attention to detail.
The detective calls upon the doctor at his surgery late one night to request his assistance in an investigation.

The detective explains that, in the army camp, the colonel of the regiment (in some editions another regiment) and his wife the wife were a seemingly happy couple; however, the colonel has died, and his wife is suspected of his murder.
The major, the detective's contact in the regiment, has explained that the colonel, while completely devoted to his wife, had a rather vindictive nature elsewhere.
He had also been subject to random fits of depression, and disliked being left alone at night.
The night of the supposed crime, the wife left for a church meeting in company with her friend, the young lady.
When she returned, she was considerably agitated and asked her maid for tea.
When the maid returned with the tea, she overheard the couple furiously arguing behind the locked morning room door.
The wife, the only one loud enough to be clearly audible, repeatedly said the words "the ancient king", "coward", and "give me back my life".
Moments later, screams rang out; when the couple's coachman entered the room through the open French windows, he found the wife collapsed and the colonel dead, bleeding from a head wound.
The key to the room was missing, and the door had to be opened by a locksmith.
The wife, temporarily insane from shock, was removed to a hospital, and the detective was called in to investigate.
The detective finds signs that a silent third party had been present; the man had left his stick in the room, his footprints in the lawn, and presumably also had taken the key.
The detective also finds the pawmarks of a short-legged, long-bodied animal on the floor, as well as signs the creature had attempted to eat the couple's pet canary.
Interrogating the young lady, the detective learns that, on the way home from the meeting, she and the wife had encountered a deformed man with a wooden box on his back.
Both he and the wife seemed badly startled; he addressed her by name, and she called him "his first name".
They spoke privately for a moment, then parted, both very upset.
After swearing her friend to silence, the wife returned home.
As the man's appearance was distinctive, the detective was soon able to discover his identity: the conjurer, a conjurer who entertained the soldiers around the garrison town.
With the doctor as a witness, the detective visits the conjurer in his lodgings.
The conjurer gladly tells his story to save the wife from being accused of murder.
Thirty years prior, he had been in the eastern colony, a soldier in the regiment with the colonel, then a Sergeant.
Both men loved the wife, but she was devoted to the conjurer, despite her father's disapproval.
The couple remained true to each other, nonetheless, but when the Indian Rebellion of 1857 erupted, the regiment found themselves cut off from supplies.

The conjurer volunteered to go for help, and the colonel gave him information on how to safely sneak through the enemy lines; however, the colonel, wishing to have the wife to himself, secretly alerted the insurgents that the conjurer would be passing.
The conjurer was captured, and learned from his captors of the betrayal.
Over the years, he was repeatedly enslaved and tortured, resulting in his deformed back and legs.
Finally escaping, he lived for many years in the eastern colony as a conjurer, preferring the wife and his fellow soldiers to think he had been killed in action instead of seeing his deformity.
In his old age, wanting to see the home country and be around soldiers again, he saved enough money to travel to the garrison town, not realizing his own old regiment was currently stationed there.
Unexpectedly running into the wife, he had admitted her husband's betrayal to her, then secretly followed her to her house.

Seeing the colonel arguing with the wife, the conjurer had entered the room through the French windows to defend her, but the colonel had instantly died of apoplexy at the mere sight of the conjurer alive and struck his head on the fender as he fell.
The wife screamed and fainted.
In the chaos, the conjurer's pet mongoose the animal escaped his wooden box, and ran up the curtain after the canary.
Reflexively pocketing the door key, the conjurer recaptured the animal and fled the scene, afraid he would be accused of murder.

Like the conjurer, the detective is hesitant to rake up a 30-year-old military scandal; learning that the medical examiner has confirmed the colonel died of apoplexy, the detective keeps the conjurer's story secret for the time being.

Questioned by the doctor about the wife's use of the name "the ancient king" when no one involved in the case went by that name, the detective decides that the wife must have been comparing her husband to the scriptural ancient king, who arranged the murder of the soldier to have the soldier's wife the desired woman.
The detective and the companion are consulted by the physician, a young general practitioner whose specialty is neurological disorders.
Two years prior, having been a brilliant student but lacking the money to set up in practice, the physician agreed to a strange business proposition put forward by an investor.
The investor bought a house in a city street, furnished it, paid servants, and purchased everything the physician could need; All the physician had to do was set up a consulting room.
Each evening, the investor would check the day's accounts and take three-quarters of the doctor's earnings, put it in his strong box, and leave the remainder for the doctor.
Another unusual condition is having the investor to live in the house as a permanent resident patient due to his heart trouble.
The investment has made the investor rich, and the physician has become a well-known, respected doctor.

However, some months ago, the investor panicked after claiming to have read a newspaper article about a nearby burglary; he insisted upon stronger locks and other stringent security measures, and also refused to leave the house for several weeks, only recently resuming his habit of taking his evening walk.
Secondly, the evening before the physician's visit to the detective, an elderly Russian nobleman and his son consulted the doctor, due to the father's complaint of catalepsy.
The son remained in the waiting room while the father spoke to the doctor – however, the old gentleman suffered a cataleptic attack while in the consulting room.
The physician spent several minutes looking for some amyl nitrite, but both father and son were gone when he returned with it.
They visited again the next evening, apologizing for mistakenly believing the consultation was over the day before.
The physician again consulted the father while the son waited outside.
After the pair left, the investor returned from his walk, found footprints in his room, and entered into a state of panic again, insisting the physician go and fetch the detective to his aid.

The detective and the companion return to the city street with the doctor, but the investor refuses to admit to the detective why he is obviously afraid for his life, or why there are men pursuing him.
He instead pretends that he believes they are unknown burglars, who are after the fortune he keeps in the chest at the foot of his bed (which he does since he does not trust bankers).
The detective eventually leaves in disgust, advising the investor that he cannot help him unless he tells the truth.
However, by studying the footprints, the detective has been able to confirm the doctor's story and eliminate him as a suspect.

It was the nobleman's son who twice entered the room, first while his father (most likely) pretended to have a cataleptic seizure the day before, then a second time while the doctor was kept busy consulting the father, leaving wet footprints since it was rather rainy outside the second day.
However, the investor had been out walking both times, inadvertently frustrating his enemies.
The next morning, the detective and the companion return to the city street at a summons from the physician.
The investor has been found dead, having apparently hanged himself during the night.

The detective and the inspector of the police headquarters examine the scene; the detective is able to find convincing evidence (different brands of cigars/ash, footprints, tools left behind) that three intruders were in the house that night.
Two of them are the supposed "Russian nobleman" and his son; the third is unknown.
Signs indicate the trio were admitted into the house by a confederate, most likely the newly hired page.
They then held a sort of mock-judicial proceeding against the investor, "condemned" him, hanged him, and retreated, the confederate barring the door behind them.

Taking a photograph of the investor, the detective leaves to consult the police headquarters' files, and returns with the news that he has identified the investor as the informer, one of the five members of the bank-robbing gang.
The others were the first gang member, the second gang member, the third gang member, and the fourth gang member.
After the gang committed a massive robbery in 1875 where the bank's caretaker was killed, the informer turned his four comrades in to the police in exchange for leniency.
The first gang member was hanged for murdering the caretaker, and the other three got lengthy prison terms of 15 years apiece.
To hide from them, the informer changed his name to an alias and moved in with the physician.
However, the informer's comrades qualified for parole several years before their term was up; his first panic was when he read of their unexpected early release from prison.
As he feared, they eventually hunted him down and murdered him to avenge the first gang member.
The informer was unable to tell the detective the truth of the matter because he would have had to reveal his true identity, which, given the circumstances, he was too frightened and ashamed to do.
The inspector arrests the page and instigates a search, but the second gang member, the third gang member, and the fourth gang member escape the country.
The case against the page breaks down for lack of evidence, and the three murderers are suspected to have died in the wreck of the ship, a steamer, off the Portuguese coast.

One summer evening, while engaged in an aimless conversation that has come round to the topic of hereditary attributes, the doctor learns that the detective, far from being a one-off in his powers of observation and deductive reasoning, in fact has an elder brother whose skills the detective claims outstrip even his own.
As a consequence of this, the doctor becomes acquainted with the gentlemen's club and his friend's brother, the older man.

The older man, as the doctor learns, does not have the energy of his younger brother and as a consequence is uninterested in using his great skills for detective work: In spite of his inertia, the older man has often delivered the correct answer to a problem that the detective has brought to him.
On this occasion, however, it is the older man who has need to consult the detective.
The translator, a Greek interpreter and neighbour of the older man, tells of a rather unnerving experience he has recently gone through.
The translator was called upon one evening by a man, the kidnapper, to go to a house, supposedly in a fashionable district, to translate on a business matter.
On the way there in the kidnapper's coach, the translator noticed that the windows were papered over so that he could not see where he was.
The kidnapper also produced a bludgeon, laying it beside him as an implied threat.
The translator protested, saying that what the kidnapper was doing was unlawful.
The kidnapper replied that he would make it up to the translator, but threatened him with unspecified retribution should the evening's business ever be made public.
For approximately two hours they drove, at last arriving at a house.
It was dark, and the translator got only a general impression of a large property as he was hustled out of the coach and into the house.
The house itself was poorly lit, but the translator made out that it was quite big.

In the room into which he was led by the kidnapper and another, nervous, giggling gentleman—whose name is later discovered to be that of the accomplice—the translator noticed a deep-pile carpet, a high marble mantel, and a suit of Japanese armour.
Another man was brought into the room.
He was thin and emaciated and had sticking plaster all over his face, and a bandage sealing his mouth.
The translator was sly enough to observe that his kidnappers were utterly ignorant of Greek, and used this to find out some information.
While the kidnapper and his companion had the translator translate demands that the man sign some papers, the translator added his own short questions to the dialogue.

The man not only answered the kidnapper that he would never sign these papers, but he also answered the translator that his name was a Greek one, that he had been in the city for three weeks, that he had no idea what house he was in, and that his captors at the house were starving him.
He wrote all his answers, unable as he was to speak through the sticking plaster.
Much could be inferred from the captive's answers to the kidnapper, too.
Evidently, the kidnapper was trying to coerce the captive into signing over property to him, and a woman was also involved.
The kidnapper had warned the captive that his obstinacy would do her no good.
The translator would have extracted the whole story from the stranger had the woman herself not burst in unexpectedly, but even that event furnished new information.
She recognised the captive as "his first name", whereupon he managed to get the bandage off his mouth and he called her "her pet name".
They both behaved as though neither had expected to see the other.
The translator was ushered back into the coach for another interminable ride and was deposited far from his home on a public common.
He made it to a railway junction just in time for the last train to the main station.
He had presented his story at the gentlemen's club to the older man, who asks his brother the detective to look into it.
An advertisement has been placed begging the public for information.
It yields a result.
A respondent knows the woman in question, and she is currently residing at a villa, a house in the suburb.
The detective and his brother the older man, who received the message from the respondent, decide that they must go to the suburb to see about this.
The doctor comes, too, and they decide to pick up the police inspector, and the translator as well in case some translating needs to be done.
They find, however, that he has already been picked up, by a nervous, giggling man brandishing a bludgeon.
The detective knows that this means the thugs know that the translator has betrayed them.
After the necessary legal procedures for securing a search warrant have been completed, the group proceeds to the suburb only to discover that the house has been abandoned.
Tracks indicate that a fully loaded coach has recently pulled out of the drive.

Breaking in, they discover the translator and the captive bound in a closed room where some charcoal has been lit to gas the two of them: the translator recovers thanks to the doctor's timely intervention, but the captive is already dead.
Apparently, the captive never signed any papers.
The client, a young foreign ministry employee from a provincial town, sends a letter to the companion, a former schoolfellow of his.
The client indicates something has caused him a nine-week attack of brain fever; now that he has recovered, he begs the companion to bring the detective to his aid.
The detective views the letter, and deduces that it was dictated to, and written by, a woman.
He accompanies the companion to the country residence, the client's house.
There, they are greeted by the future brother-in-law, the brother of the client's fiancée, the young woman (the writer of the letter).
The future brother-in-law shows them in to see the client, who is still recovering from his long illness and being nursed by the young woman.
The client lays the case before the detective.
Two months earlier, his uncle and superior in the foreign ministry, the statesman, had ordered him to copy an important naval treaty between the home country and a foreign kingdom.
The treaty was to be kept secret, for many foreign governments would want to read it.
The client told no one of this assignment, and waited until the building was empty except for the doorkeeper, the commissionaire, and his wife, who did the charring.
The client then copied the papers as quickly as he could but it soon became apparent the task would take most of the night.
The client rang the bell for some coffee.
The doorkeeper's wife took the order to her husband; much later, the client came downstairs to investigate why he had not received his coffee and found the doorkeeper had fallen asleep.
The bell to the client's office rang; realizing someone was in the room, the client dashed back upstairs and found the naval treaty gone.
There were no hiding places, and no one could have passed the client on the front stair, so the thief must have come and gone by the back stair.
The client, a constable, and the inspector of the police headquarters frantically searched for the thief without success.
The client had a nervous breakdown and was escorted back to the country residence.
As the future brother-in-law's bedroom was best suited for a sickroom, the future brother-in-law was forced out of it by the doctor.
The client has remained there, nursed by the young woman by day and a hired nurse by night.
The detective starts the investigation at the foreign ministry, interviewing both the statesman and the inspector.
He learns that the doorkeeper and his wife and a clerk, a co-worker, were suspected and then cleared.
The statesman informs him that no foreign government has received the treaty yet, which seems odd since nine weeks have passed.

The detective also discovers that the young woman and the future brother-in-law were never meant to be long-term guests; they had come down for a few days' visit when the tragedy occurred but had stayed so the young woman could nurse her fiancée.
Returning to the country residence the next day, the detective learns that the client dispensed with the hired nurse the evening before.
Later that same evening, someone tried to break into the client's sickroom window with a knife.
The client immediately roused the household, but the burglar got away.
Unbeknownst to the client or the future brother-in-law, the detective orders the young woman to stay in the sickroom until bedtime and to lock the door behind her when she leaves.
He then arranges that the client and the companion should go to the city.
The companion takes the client back to the detective's lodgings, but neither can understand the detective's actions.
The next morning, the detective arrives with disheveled clothes and a bandaged hand.
At the breakfast table, he pretends to have found nothing, but then arranges for the landlady to serve the client the treaty on his breakfast plate.
The client is overjoyed to have it back, nearly fainting with relief.
The detective had realized the future brother-in-law was responsible.
The sickroom was formerly his bedroom, and only someone in the house could have known when no nurse would be on guard.
The future brother-in-law had come to the client's office to ask if the client was coming home, rung the bell, then found the treaty.
As the future brother-in-law had some stock exchange debts to pay, he stole the treaty, intending to sell it, and hid it under the floorboards of his bedroom.
However, the client's breakdown and the two nurses on hand in the room had kept the future brother-in-law from getting at the treaty for weeks.
The first chance he had, the future brother-in-law had tried and failed to steal the treaty back.
The detective had kept the young woman in the room so the future brother-in-law could not get at the treaty during the daytime.
After she left, the future brother-in-law broke in and retrieved the treaty, but the detective ambushed him, and boxed him for the papers.
An injured detective arrives at the companion's residence one evening, having escaped three separate murder attempts that day.
The detective reveals to the companion he has been tracking the criminal mastermind and his organisation for months, who are responsible for most of the crimes orchestrated in the city.

As the detective is close to snaring them all and delivering them to the police, the criminal mastermind visits the detective at the lodgings earlier that day and warns him to withdraw from his pursuit of justice against him.

The detective admits that the criminal mastermind could thwart his plans given his great mind that could rival his, and plans to flee to the continent while the police capture the criminal mastermind and his gang.
The detective invites the companion to join him on the trip.

The detective then gives him unusual instructions intended to hide his tracks to the boat train at the main station before leaving the companion's house by climbing over the back wall in the garden, paranoid that he might be followed.
The next day, the companion follows the detective's instructions and finds himself waiting in the reserved first-class coach for his friend, who is disguised as an elderly Italian priest.

The detective informs the companion that the rooms at the lodgings had been set on fire the previous night, in an unsuccessful attempt to both kill him and destroy the evidence he had collected against the criminal mastermind.
As the boat train pulls out of the main station, the detective spots the criminal mastermind on the platform trying to stop the train.
The detective deduces that the criminal mastermind has tracked the companion despite extraordinary precautions.

Changing their planned route, the detective and the companion alight at an intermediate town, hiding behind the luggage as the criminal mastermind (who had chartered a special one-coach train) passes them in pursuit.

After the detective and the companion have crossed the sea strait and made their way to a border city via a foreign capital, the detective receives a message from the city police that most of the criminal mastermind's gang have been arrested in the home country, but the criminal mastermind has escaped and is in pursuit of the detective on the continent.
He urges the companion to return to the home country as he considers himself a very dangerous companion, but the companion chooses to stay with him.
The two continue to an alpine village in a mountainous country and visit the waterfall.
At the waterfall, a boy hands the companion a letter, saying that there is a dying Englishwoman at the hotel who seeks an English doctor.
The detective sends the companion back to tend to her and remains at the waterfall.
Upon reaching the hotel, the companion discovers that he has been tricked and rushes back to aid the detective.

At the waterfall, he only finds two sets of footprints that lead to the end of the path, where he uncovers other signs of a violent struggle and a note from the detective explaining that he knew of the hoax but chose to fight the criminal mastermind himself.
It is all too clear to the companion that the detective and the criminal mastermind have both fallen to their deaths down the gorge while locked in mortal combat and their bodies cannot be recovered.

The companion ends his narrative by saying that the criminal mastermind's gang are all convicted on the strength of evidence secured by the detective, and that despite the criminal mastermind's brother defending the Professor's memory, the companion will regard the detective as the best and the wisest man he had ever known.
On the night of 30 March, an apparently unsolvable locked-room murder takes place in the city: the killing of the young nobleman.
The companion visits the murder scene.
He runs into an elderly deformed book collector, later revealed as the detective in disguise, to his astonishment.

Contrary to what the companion believed, the detective survived his encounter with the criminal mastermind at the waterfall, faked his fall and spent the next few years travelling to various parts of the world, dismantling the remnants of the criminal mastermind's gang.
That evening, they enter an abandoned building known as the empty house whose front room overlooks the detective's street.
The detective's room can be seen across the street.
In the window is a lifelike waxwork bust of the detective in profile.
At approximately midnight, a sniper, who has taken the bait, fires a specialised air gun, scoring a direct hit on the detective's dummy.
The inspector arrests the gunman, who is revealed as the colonel, the young nobleman's whist partner and murderer.
The detective describes the colonel as having been "the second most dangerous man in the city" while the criminal mastermind was still alive.
The detective speculates that the young nobleman had caught the colonel cheating at cards, and threatened to expose his dishonourable behaviour.
The colonel, who earned a living playing cards crookedly, got rid of the one man who could rob him of his livelihood.
The detective and the companion are visited by the accused man, a young lawyer from the home suburb who has been accused of murdering one of his clients – the builder.
The accused man explains to the detective that the builder had come to his office the day before and asked him to draw up his will in proper legal form.
To his surprise, the builder was making him the sole beneficiary to a considerable bequest.
Later, the accused man went to the builder's house in the neighbouring suburb to deliver the will and go over some additional documents.
The accused man left quite late and stayed at a local inn.
On the train the next morning, he read in the newspaper about the apparent murder of the builder and that the police were looking for him.

The evidence against the accused man is quite damning: bloodstains were found in the builder's study and on a walking stick the accused man had left there, and behind the house is a pile of dry timber burnt to ashes and smelling of burnt flesh.
The inspector, who comes to arrest the accused man, gloats in the apparent knowledge that he is on the right track.
The detective begins his own investigation by going to the home suburb instead of the neighbouring suburb.
There he learns that the accused man's mother was once engaged to the builder but broke up with him once she found out his cruel nature.
The detective also notes that the builder's draft will was written in a very haphazard fashion, as if he did not care about its content.
He also discovers large payments from the builder's bank account to a "mystery payee".
The detective then visits the builder's house, where he inspects the study.
The inspector produces the builder's trouser buttons, found in the ashes of the fire.
The detective fears the worst: "All my instincts are in one direction, and all the facts are in another."
Still, the detective suspects the builder's housekeeper is deliberately withholding information.
The next morning, a bloody thumbprint is found at the builder's house that matches the accused man's.
This seems to be conclusive, as the inspector smugly notes.
However, the detective is sure the thumbprint was not there in his previous inspection, and the accused man could not have left it as he has been in police custody.
The detective tells the inspector there is another important witness to see, whom he offers to produce.
The inspector is dismissive but lets the detective proceed.
The detective starts a small, smoky fire in the upper hall of the house and has the constables shout "Fire!"
The builder emerges alive from a hidden chamber at the end of the hall.
The detective had deduced its existence by measuring the halls, noting that the upper one was several feet shorter than the lower.

The builder staged his apparent murder to gain revenge against the accused man's mother; he started the timber fire, threw his trousers and some small animals into the flames, and planted the bloodstains.
He tries to pass off his actions as a practical joke but is taken into custody, along with the housekeeper as an accomplice.
"The mystery payee" is an alias to be used by the builder to evade his creditors.
The detective remarks to the inspector that the builder's plot was nearly perfect, but he went one step too far by planting the thumbprint (from a wax seal that the accused man had pressed).
"He wished to improve what was already perfect," says the detective, "and so he ruined everything."
